title: Unbought. Unbossed. First Black Woman in Congress.

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

beats.text: Born in Brooklyn in 1924 to Caribbean immigrants, she spent part of her childhood in Barbados.
A nursery school teacher, she won a seat in the New York State Assembly in 1964.
In 1968, she ran for Congress under one slogan: Unbought and Unbossed. She won. The first Black woman ever elected.
They put the Brooklyn congresswoman on the Agriculture Committee. She refused, and fought until they moved her.
In 1971, she co-founded the Congressional Black Caucus.
In 1972, she ran for president: the first Black candidate, and the first woman, to seek the Democratic nomination.

visual.caption: Announcing her run for president, January 25, 1972

beats.text: At the convention she won 152 delegate votes, about ten percent.

visual.title: 152 votes
visual.caption: Democratic National Convention, Miami Beach, July 12, 1972

beats.text: She served seven terms, until 1983, and helped create the WIC program for mothers and children.
She died on New Year's Day, 2005. In 2015, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

facts.claim: Born 30 Nov 1924, Brooklyn; father from Guyana, mother from Barbados; lived in Barbados as a child (about 1929-34).
Nursery school teacher, day care director; New York State Assembly from 1964/65 to 1968.
Elected 1968, NY 12th district; motto Unbought and Unbossed; first Black woman elected to Congress.
Assigned to Agriculture; protested to Speaker McCormack and the caucus; reassigned to Veterans' Affairs.
Founding member of the Congressional Black Caucus (1971) and the National Women's Political Caucus.
1972: first Black candidate to seek a major party's presidential nomination, first woman to seek the Democratic nomination.
152 delegate votes at the 1972 convention, about 10 percent.
Seven terms, 1969-1983; worked to expand food stamps and helped create WIC.
Died 1 Jan 2005, Ormond Beach, Florida; posthumous Presidential Medal of Freedom 2015.
